hero.title: About Me
hero.subtitle: Builder notes behind a trade-basics co-learning project

intro.title: Who I Am
intro.content: I am the developer of this site and a trader still learning every day. This project started as my own journal and evolved into a structured workflow for recording, reviewing, and improving decisions with others.

motivation.title: Why I Built This
motivation.paragraph1: I used to repeat the same mistakes in emotional, low-discipline trades. Over time, I learned the real issue was not a lack of information, but the lack of a consistent process I could review.
motivation.paragraph2: This site is not built to promise quick wins. It is a practical training environment: log each decision, review it regularly, and refine your rules to reduce repeated errors while moving toward long-term goals like financial freedom and passive income.

pyramid.name: Pyramid (4-3-2-1)
pyramid.description: The most robust strategy, emphasizing a solid foundation. 40% base position at fair valuation or trend confirmation, then scale in.
cons: If base position is poorly timed, adding too fast during decline may lead to being trapped

pyramidVariant.name: Pyramid Variant (2-2-3-2-1)
pyramidVariant.description: Split the base position to reduce initial entry risk, suitable for volatile markets.
cons: Need more time to observe market

rectangular.name: Rectangular (3-3-3-1)
rectangular.description: Buy 30% three times, keep 10% cash as 'emergency fund' for black swan events.

invertedPyramid.name: Inverted Pyramid (1-2-3-4)
invertedPyramid.description: Minimal initial investment, then significantly increase. Suitable when highly confident in the target and expecting significant upside.
cons: Larger loss if judgment is wrong

seasonality.title: US Stock Market Seasonality
seasonality.subtitle: Based on historical data from 1950 to present, analyzing S&P 500 monthly seasonality patterns
seasonality.strongPeriodDesc: November to April (historically higher returns than May to October)
seasonality.weakPeriodDesc: May to October ("Sell in May and go away" phenomenon)

recommendationsList.0: Seasonality is for reference only, suitable for supplementing long-term strategies (e.g., dollar-cost averaging)
recommendationsList.1: Short-term trading should consider current macroeconomic factors (interest rates, economic data, elections), risk management, and diversification
recommendationsList.2: Historical data shows "time in the market" is far superior to "timing the market"

seasonality.disclaimer: Seasonality is for reference only and should supplement long-term strategies (e.g., dollar-cost averaging). Short-term trading should consider current macroeconomic factors (interest rates, economic data, elections), risk management, and diversification. Historical data shows "time in the market" is far superior to "timing the market".
seasonality.dataSource: Data source: S&P 500 historical data from 1950 to present (Visual Capitalist / YCharts)

jan.characteristics: Strong start to the year, common "January Effect" (more pronounced in small caps)

apr.characteristics: One of the strongest months, post-tax season rally

reasons.1: Low liquidity susceptible to news impact

reasons.0: Fiscal year end (many funds settle 9/30) rebalancing
reasons.2: Back to school / corporate budget pressure

reasons.1: Historical events (1929, 1987, 2008) but average often rebounds

strongPeriod.name: Best Six Months
strongPeriod.description: November to April (historically higher returns than May to October)
strongPeriod.strategy: Supports "Sell in May and go away" strategy, but long-term holding still outperforms timing

weakPeriod.name: Weak Period
weakPeriod.description: May to October ("Sell in May and go away" phenomenon)
weakPeriod.strategy: Volatility is higher in autumn (especially September-October), relatively stable in summer

financialFreedom.whatIsFireNumberDesc: FIRE Number is your financial freedom target based on annual expenses and withdrawal rate. For example: 600k annual expenses, 4% withdrawal rate = 600k ÷ 4% = 15 million.
financialFreedom.aboutWithdrawalRateDesc: The 4% rule comes from US historical backtesting, showing that withdrawing 4% annually has a high probability of portfolio lasting 30+ years. 3% is more conservative, 5% is more aggressive but riskier.
